title: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (1 of 7)
hook: a lump of clay, a pot, a cup, a lamp: how many things are on the potter's shelf?
tomorrow: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Last week ended the three paths, with the line who am I? And the Ashtavakra Gita's verse: as you think, so you become. Today, two weeks on two great schools, starting with the first. Day two hundred eighty-one.

Picture a potter's shelf. A water pot, a cup, a little oil lamp, a toy elephant for a child. Four things, right? Different shapes, different names, different uses. You'd pay different prices for them. Now look again. What are they, actually? Clay. All of it. The names are real enough; you'd never drink from the lamp. But underneath the names, there's one stuff. The Upanishads used exactly this picture, thousands of years ago, and a teacher named Shankara built a whole way of seeing on it.
screen: `A POT, A CUP, A LAMP, A TOY.` → `FOUR THINGS?` → `ALL OF IT, CLAY.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a father, Uddalaka, teaches his son: by knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The change is only a word, a name; the truth is, it's clay. Then he goes further. In the beginning, he says, there was only being, one without a second. From that line comes a word: advaita. Dvaita means two, duality. A means not. Advaita: not two. Here's the subtle part. It doesn't say one. Teachers of this school are careful about that. One suggests something you could count, one thing sitting next to nothing. Not-two just refuses the split. Between you and the world, between you and God, between the pot and the clay: not two. The teacher most tied to this school is Shankara. Tradition says he was born in Kaladi, in Kerala, became a monk as a boy, walked the length of India, wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras, founded monasteries in several directions of India, and died at about thirty-two. Tradition dates him to around 800; many scholars place him somewhat earlier. His claim, put simply: there is one reality, Brahman, pure awareness. What you most deeply are, the atman, is not different from it. The world of many things is how that one reality appears. Now an honest frame for the next two weeks. Advaita is one great school of Vedanta. Right after it, we'll meet schools that say the soul and God stay two, forever. Millions of Hindus hold each. Neither is the Hindu view, and we won't rank them.
screen: `KNOW THE CLAY, KNOW THE POTS.` · `ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.` · `A-DVAITA: NOT TWO.` · `SHANKARA'S ONE REALITY, BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look around the room for a moment before closing your eyes. Many things: a chair, a wall, a window, your hands. Then close your eyes, and notice that all of them, right now, are appearing in one awareness. The sounds too. The body's feelings too. Many shapes, one field they all show up in. You don't have to believe anything about it. Just notice: many things, and one seeing. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Advaita. Not two: the teaching, tied to Shankara, that the self and Brahman, the one reality, are not different, as pots are not different from clay.
Your line: not two. Today, pick up one ordinary object, a mug, a pen, and see if you can see the clay under the cup: what it's made of, under its name. Day two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta is taught in monasteries associated with Shankara, such as Sringeri, and by many modern teachers; students study the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras with Shankara's commentaries and contemplate the non-difference of the self and Brahman.

myth: it means not two; teachers deliberately avoid saying one.
the clay-and-pots picture comes from the Chandogya Upanishad
Uddalaka tells his son: know one lump of clay, and you know all that's made of clay.
all Hindus hold the Advaita view
it's one great school of Vedanta; other schools teach that soul and God remain two.

fork.setup: you're on a potter's shelf: a pot, a cup, a lamp, a toy. the Upanishad asks how many things there are. what's its answer?
options: one stuff, clay, with four names.
fork.reveal: clay, with different names and shapes. the names are real enough to use; the truth underneath is one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Advaita means everything is one blob.
what it means: not two: the self and the one reality, Brahman, are not different, as pots aren't different from clay.

what a scholar hears: 'one without a second' is Chandogya 6.2.1 (ekam evādvitīyam); the clay example is 6.1.4; Advaita as a school predates Shankara (Gaudapada's Karika), and his dates are debated (traditionally 788–820).

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4 (clay and what is made of clay)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1 (being, one only, without a second)

notes: Shankara's life (Kaladi, monk as a boy, monasteries, death at about 32) is traditional; dates debated. Please check phrasing.
'Pure awareness' as a gloss for Brahman simplifies sat-chit-ananda; confirm.
The framing 'neither is the Hindu view, and we won't rank them' follows the outline's 'electives, never ranked'.
